entry.title: TULIP: Permissionless Decentralized Identity
entry.summary:
A decentralized identity system offers significant advantages over those managed by central authorities. Traditional identity solutions controlled by coordinators can restrict user autonomy and enable data omission, undermining trust and personal control. Systems that leverage cryptographic keys, such as secp256k1 keys paired with Schnorr (BIP 340) signatures, provide a foundation for pseudonymous identities, allowing users to sign every event they publish for enhanced security and verifiability.
One of the persistent challenges in these systems is secure key rotation. While many platforms recognize its importance, few have implemented robust, widely adopted mechanisms due to the inherent complexity. The proposed solution addresses this by utilizing the Bitcoin blockchain not just as a record of transactions, but as a global, tamper-resistant authority for timestamping and ordering identity key state changes. This approach ensures that the most current signing key status is always anchored to the blockchain, eliminating reliance on external databases or centralized registries.
The design prioritizes scalability by assuming that most users will rarely need to interact directly with the blockchain. Only when a signing key is compromised or a high-value identity requires protection does an on-chain native taproot transaction become necessary. Identity rotation is achieved through a precommitted “taproot chain,” where each new state references a tweaked taproot output acting as the next signing key and policy anchor. This method, referred to as a "tulip," requires advance commitment to all potential future rotations and keys at the moment of identity creation. When it becomes necessary to rotate, the subsequent key—ideally stored securely offline—is brought online to sign and broadcast the transaction, updating the identity’s operational credentials.
Recovery mechanisms are also built into the protocol. Should a recovery be needed, a new Taproot chain can be initiated under separate conditions. However, if an attacker meets the requirements of the recovery script and possesses knowledge of the current tulip descriptor, they could assume control of the identity. In such cases, recourse would involve leveraging Web of Trust (WoT) strategies and revoking the compromised identity.
The interpretation and value of an identity established through this system are left to the discretion of individual applications and services. Various use cases range from managing rate limits for large language models, controlling testnet faucet distributions, facilitating account creation for games, supporting reputation-backed media content, to moderating contributions in open-source software projects. These applications can apply different filters and policies based on the attributes embedded within the identity protocol.
For further technical details, a comprehensive whitepaper is accessible at [tuliproot.com](https://tuliproot.com/). The protocol envisions integration with WoT applications, enabling more secure verification and authentication workflows. To support efficient indexing and monitoring of relevant transactions, the proposal includes using a 4-byte witness header. This allows nodes or service providers to track important state changes without exhaustive scanning. If no on-chain activity exists for a given identity, off-chain proofs can demonstrate the inception and integrity of the identity, using techniques like KZG commitments for compactness and future publishability on-chain.
Implementing this protocol would require either running a specialized node capable of scanning and indexing the Bitcoin blockchain or relying on third-party services to provide this functionality. By balancing on-chain footprint minimization with robust cryptographic guarantees, this approach aims to create a scalable, user-controlled, and pseudonymous identity infrastructure.
